items.title: Standard-normal CDF, tail, and quantile identities for power calculations
items.statement: Assume AC. Let \(Z\sim N(0,1)\) and \(\Phi(x)=P(Z\le x)\). Then \(\Phi\) is continuous and strictly increasing, with limits \(0\) and \(1\) at \(-\infty\) and \(+\infty\); \(P(Z=x)=0\) for every \(x\in\mathbb R\); and \(\Phi(-x)=1-\Phi(x)\). For each \(q\in(0,1)\), there is a unique real \(z_q\) with \(\Phi(z_q)=q\), and \(z_{1-q}=-z_q\), in particular \(z_{1/2}=0\).

items.axiom_use: AC is used by the standard-normal law and implies countable choice; countable choice is used only with the zero-width-box theorem to show singleton normal probabilities vanish.

items.title: A nonempty set of positive integers has a least member
items.statement: Let \(S\subseteq\mathbb N_{\ge1}\) be nonempty. Then there is a unique \(n_*\in S\) such that \(n_*\le n\) for every \(n\in S\).

references.title: Gary W. Oehlert, A First Course in Design and Analysis of Experiments, Chapter 7, §7.1, printed pp. 149–150

items.title: Ceilings give the least positive integer meeting a real threshold

references.title: Emily Riehl, Category Theory in Context, Example 4.1.7, printed p. 134

items.statement:
Identify integers and naturals with their canonical copies in the reals. For every real $x$, put $\lceil x\rceil=-\lfloor-x\rfloor$, using [[lem-integer-part]]. Then $\lceil x\rceil$ is an integer, $x\le\lceil x\rceil$, and
$$\lceil x\rceil\le m\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x\le m\qquad(m\in\mathbb Z).$$
For $a\ge0$, the least positive integer $n$ with $n\ge a$ is $\max\{1,\lceil a\rceil\}$. In particular $\lceil0\rceil=0$, and $\lceil k\rceil=k$ for every integer $k$.
items.strategy: Derive the ceiling inequalities from the proved floor theorem and integer discreteness.

items.title: Power and sample-size planning specifications
items.statement: Let \(\mathsf E_d=((\mathcal X_d,\mathcal A_d),\Theta,(P_{\theta,d})_{\theta\in\Theta})\) be the specified statistical experiment for each candidate plan \(d\) in a nonempty or empty candidate set \(\mathcal D\). A plan records its sampling or assignment law, a permitted allocation vector \(\mathbf n(d)=(n_1,\ldots,n_g)\) for an integer \(g\ge1\), with nonnegative integer counts \(n_j\), and its total sample size \(n(d)=\sum_{j=1}^g n_j\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\). Which allocations are permitted, including any positive lower bounds, capacity limits, or costs, is part of \(\mathcal D\).
items.strategy: Specify model, test or interval criteria, effect or precision target, integer allocations, and the extensional least feasible sample size.

references.title: Gary W. Oehlert, A First Course in Design and Analysis of Experiments, Chapter 7, §§7.1–7.7, printed pp. 149–161
NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, §7.2.2.2, PDF pp. 2019–2021

items.title: Both tails determine power for the known-variance two-sided normal z-test
items.statement:
Assume AC. Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be mutually independent with common law $N(\mu,\sigma^2)$, where $n\ge1$ and $\sigma>0$. For the simple null $H_0:\mu=\mu_0$ against the two-sided alternative $H_1:\mu\ne\mu_0$, let $Z_n=\sqrt n(\bar X_n-\mu_0)/\sigma$, let $c_\alpha=z_{1-\alpha/2}$ for $\alpha\in(0,1)$, and reject when $|Z_n|>c_\alpha$. This test has size $\alpha$. At $\mu=\mu_0+\delta$, where $\delta\in\mathbb R$, its rejection probability (the power function evaluated at this parameter) is
$$1-\Phi(c_\alpha-\lambda)+\Phi(-c_\alpha-\lambda), \qquad \lambda=\frac{\sqrt n\,\delta}{\sigma}.$$
For $\delta\ne0$ this is power at the stated alternative; for $\delta=0$ it is the null rejection probability. The first term is the upper-tail rejection probability and the second is the lower-tail rejection probability.

references.title: Gary W. Oehlert, A First Course in Design and Analysis of Experiments, Chapter 7, §§7.1–7.4, printed pp. 149–159

items.title: Finite-candidate power and sample-size search
items.statement: Input a planning specification [[def-power-and-sample-size-planning-specification]], a finite ordered list \(d_1,\ldots,d_m\) of its candidate plans with \(n(d_1)\le\cdots\le n(d_m)\), and an exact evaluator that terminates on each listed plan and returns true exactly when that plan meets all requested power, precision, allocation, and resource conditions. The list order among equal-size plans is part of the input.
items.strategy: Inspect the finite candidate list in nondecreasing size order and return the first exact feasible plan.

references.title: Gary W. Oehlert, A First Course in Design and Analysis of Experiments, Chapter 7, §§7.1 and 7.3–7.4, printed pp. 149–150, 153–159

items.title: Exact power and least sample size for a known-variance normal z-test
items.statement:
Assume AC. Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be mutually independent with common law $N(\mu,\sigma^2)$, where $n\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}$, $\sigma>0$, and $\mu\in\mathbb R$. Fix $\mu_0\in\mathbb R$, $\alpha,\beta_{\rm II}\in(0,1)$, and $\delta>0$, and put $\mu_1=\mu_0+\delta$. Observe $\bar X_n=n^{-1}\sum_iX_i$ in the one-dimensional experiment with law $N(\mu,\sigma^2/n)$. For the upper-tail test of $H_0:\mu\le\mu_0$ against $H_1:\mu>\mu_0$ with rejection rule
$$
\varphi_n(x)=\mathbf 1\!\left\{\frac{\sqrt n(x-\mu_0)}{\sigma}>z_{1-\alpha}\right\},
$$
the test size is $\alpha$, and its power at any $\mu$ is
$$
\pi_n(\mu)=\Phi\!\left(\frac{\sqrt n(\mu-\mu_0)}{\sigma}-z_{1-\alpha}\right).
$$
The least positive integer sample size attaining target power $1-\beta_{\rm II}$ at $\mu_1$, with candidate sizes $\mathbb N_{\ge1}$, is
$$
n_*=\max\!\left\{1,\left\lceil \left(\frac{\sigma}{\delta}\right)^2
\max\!\left\{0,z_{1-\alpha}+z_{1-\beta_{\rm II}}\right\}^{2}\right\rceil\right\}.
$$
If $z_{1-\alpha}+z_{1-\beta_{\rm II}}\le0$, every positive integer size meets the target and the least is $1$. This is an exact result for the specified known-$\sigma$ normal model; it makes no approximation or claim for an unknown-$\sigma$ $t$-test or another sampling law.

references.title: Gary W. Oehlert, A First Course in Design and Analysis of Experiments, Chapter 7, §§7.1–7.4, printed pp. 149–159
NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, §7.2.2.2, PDF pp. 2019–2021

items.title: Finite-candidate power and sample-size search is correct
items.statement: For the finite-candidate algorithm [[alg-finite-candidate-power-sample-size-search]], suppose the input list is ordered by nondecreasing total size and its evaluator returns the exact feasibility truth value for every candidate. The algorithm terminates after at most \(m\) evaluations. If it returns a plan, that plan is feasible and its total size is least among feasible plans in the supplied list; if it returns \(\text{none}\), no plan in that list is feasible. When several feasible plans have the same least size, the algorithm returns the first such plan in the supplied tie order.

references.title: Gary W. Oehlert, A First Course in Design and Analysis of Experiments, Chapter 7, §§7.1 and 7.3–7.4, printed pp. 149–150, 153–159

items.title: Search over all positive sample sizes with explicit stopping certificates

references.title: Gary W. Oehlert, A First Course in Design and Analysis of Experiments, Chapter 7 §§7.1–7.2, printed pp. 149–152; local operational formulation

items.statement:
Input the full planning specification [[def-power-and-sample-size-planning-specification]] and an exact evaluator $E$ on every positive integer $n$. Each call $E(n)$ must terminate and return a Boolean with the following meaning: $E(n)$ is true exactly when the specification has a feasible plan of total size $n$, including its sampling law/test, power or precision target, allowed allocation and resource conditions. With a fixed allocation rule this is the ordinary per-size power calculation. For several candidate plans at one size, this assumption requires exact resolution of whether any is feasible; it is not supplied by the procedure. The evaluator, and any stopping certificate below, are inputs, not a universal ability to compute probabilities of arbitrary models.

Choose one of these admissible modes.

1. **Unbounded ascending search.** Set $n=1$. Evaluate $E(n)$. If true, return $n$; otherwise replace $n$ by $n+1$ and repeat. This branch never returns $\mathrm{none}$ merely because a finite prefix failed.

2. **Certified bounded search.** Supply a nonnegative integer $B$ and a valid completeness certificate that, if any positive size is feasible, some feasible size is at most $B$. Evaluate $E(1),\ldots,E(B)$ in order, returning the first true index. If all are false, return $\mathrm{none}$; for $B=0$, return $\mathrm{none}$ immediately. The certificate is a mathematical premise covering all positive sizes, not a claim inferred from those finite evaluations. A proved feasible witness of size $B$ is one sufficient certificate.

3. **Certified infeasibility.** Supply a valid proof that $E(n)$ is false for every positive integer $n$. Return $\mathrm{none}$ without an evaluation.

The output is a sample size, not a selected allocation. Selecting a plan at that size requires an explicit witness-producing evaluator or an independently specified selection rule. The extensional target remains the least feasible positive integer, or $\mathrm{none}$ if no such integer exists. Termination properties are separate proved results; no global infeasibility decision is asserted for unrestricted black-box input.

items.title: Correctness and exact termination conditions for all-size planning search

references.title: Gary W. Oehlert, A First Course in Design and Analysis of Experiments, Chapter 7 §§7.1–7.2, printed pp. 149–152; local exact-evaluator proof

items.statement:
Use the exact terminating evaluator and admissible modes of [[alg-positive-integer-power-sample-size-search]], and let $S=\{n\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}:E(n)\text{ is true}\}$. The unbounded ascending mode terminates if and only if $S\ne\varnothing$, and then returns $\min S$ after exactly $\min S$ evaluations. If $S=\varnothing$, it continues forever and returns no value, including no $\mathrm{none}$.

With a valid finite completeness bound $B$, the bounded mode terminates after at most $B$ evaluations and returns the full-domain extensional answer: $\min S$ if $S\ne\varnothing$ and $\mathrm{none}$ if $S=\varnothing$. The certified-infeasibility mode returns that answer immediately. No monotonicity is needed for these conclusions. If feasibility is nondecreasing and $E(B)$ is true, that witness is a valid bound, but monotonicity without a crossing witness or other stopping certificate does not guarantee termination in the empty case.

items.title: An exact one-sided normal sample size and its effect-variance sensitivity
items.statement: Take any $\sigma>0$, set $\delta=\sigma$, and choose $\alpha=\beta_{\rm II}=1-\Phi(1)$. For the upper-tail test $H_0:\mu\le\mu_0$ against $\mu_1=\mu_0+\delta$, the exact planning rule gives least sample size $n_*=4$ for target power $1-\beta_{\rm II}$. At $n=4$, halving the target effect with the same $\sigma$ lowers power to $1/2$. Keeping $\delta=\sigma$ and $n=4$ but doubling the standard deviation (quadrupling the variance) also lowers power to $1/2$.

items.title: Finite power-oracle queries cannot universally certify no feasible sample size
items.statement: The claim is that there is a deterministic procedure which, for every exact Boolean feasibility oracle on all positive integers, accesses that oracle only through queries of individual sizes, terminates after finitely many queries, and returns the least feasible positive size or $\mathrm{none}$ if there is none. The claim remains false even when the oracle is promised to be nondecreasing. This is a finite-query black-box statement; it does not exclude analytic solutions or additional global certificates for specified model families.
